But when a two-month road closure cut traffic noise in one city by half, ornithologist Kwame Asante found that the gap between that city's birds and nearby rural birds stayed the same, casting doubt on the idea that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: city birds of these species sing at a higher pitch than rural birds of the same species do.
the difference in pitch between city and rural birds is inherited rather than learned over time.
traffic noise in the city fell by about half during the two months the roads were closed.
city birds raise their pitch in direct response to the level of traffic noise around them.
items.explanation: The interpretation being challenged says city birds raise their pitch in response to the traffic noise around them at the time. If so, cutting the noise in half should have narrowed the 300-hertz gap. It didn't change at all. That undercuts the moment-to-moment explanation, and this choice restates it.

A.why: The pitch gap is the observed fact, and Asante's study confirms it still holds. You chose the observation that the old interpretation explains, not the interpretation that the new evidence doubts.

B.why: This is a possible alternative explanation, not the idea under doubt, and the study never tested inheritance. The steady gap is consistent with inheritance, but it is equally consistent with learning that took place earlier in a bird's life. You landed on the new-evidence side of the 'but' and made a claim stronger than the data support.

C.why: This is a background detail of the experiment, and the passage presents it as true. It doesn't name any view that the result calls into question.

the walls of the enclosures were thinner than earlier surveys had reported.
the enclosures were designed mainly to defend their occupants from attack.

rapidly rotating asteroids are necessarily composed of one solid body.

most asteroids in the solar system are loosely bound piles of rubble.

antibody levels in the blood stay elevated for at least five years.
lung-resident T cells by themselves prevent every case of reinfection.
protection against Kessel virus fades within roughly a year of recovery.

items.stimulus: Seedlings of the desert shrub Calvera are rare beneath mature Calvera plants, and ecologists long attributed this pattern to chemistry: the shrubs' roots, they argued, release compounds that keep seeds in the surrounding soil from germinating. In a recent study, however, ecologist Dana Okafor found that Calvera seeds sown in a greenhouse germinated at nearly identical rates in soil collected beneath shrubs and in soil taken from open ground, while seeds she placed beneath living shrubs in the field were mostly carried off by rodents within days. Okafor's results therefore cast doubt on the idea that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the shrubs' roots release chemical compounds into the soil that surrounds them.
rodents sheltering beneath the shrubs eat most of the seeds that fall there.
the soil beneath the shrubs contains substances that prevent seeds from germinating.
seedlings of the shrub are uncommon in the ground beneath mature shrubs.
items.explanation: The old view says something in the soil under the shrubs stops seeds from germinating. Okafor tested that directly: seeds germinated just as well in soil taken from under the shrubs as in open-ground soil. D.why: This is the observation that both explanations are trying to account for. Neither side disputes it, and the passage states it as fact. Okafor questions why seedlings are rare under the shrubs, not whether they are.

items.stimulus: Because recordings of the Brenna Valley dialect made in the 1960s capture the dropping of word-final t chiefly in speakers then under thirty, linguists long concluded that the feature was an innovation of that generation. items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: Brenna Valley farmers born in the 1850s and 1860s dropped final t in their speech.
the dropping of final t in the dialect began with speakers who were young in the 1960s.
speakers under thirty in the 1960s dropped final t more often than older speakers did.
the spellings found in personal letters can reveal how the letters' writers actually spoke.
items.explanation: Separate the old conclusion from the evidence it rested on. The evidence was that 1960s recordings show t-dropping mostly in young speakers. The conclusion was that the feature began with that generation. Maddock's letters show the feature about seventy years earlier, among people born in the 1850s and 1860s. That attacks where the feature started, not what the recordings show. So the idea in doubt is that it began with speakers who were young in the 1960s.

A.why: This is what Maddock's letters suggest, so it sits on the wrong side of the 'however'. The blank needs the idea his findings weaken, not the new claim they support.

C.why: This is the trap that remains after you spot the old view. It restates the evidence the old view rested on, not the conclusion drawn from it. items.stimulus: Studies have repeatedly found that neighborhoods with many fast-food outlets have higher adult obesity rates than neighborhoods with few, and some public health officials have taken this as evidence that living near such outlets leads people to gain weight. neighborhoods with many fast-food outlets tend to have higher obesity.
living near fast-food outlets causes residents to gain weight.

items.explanation: The blame on the farms depended on their withdrawals cutting the lake's supply. The gauges show the supply roughly unchanged, which removes that link. The doubted idea is that the withdrawals reduced what reaches the lake.

A.why: The passage states the increase in withdrawals as fact, and the gauges don't challenge it. The data undercuts what the withdrawals did, not whether they grew.

B.why: Rising evaporation is reported next to the shrinking, but 'the only reason' is strength creep. Nothing in the passage rules out other causes, and anyway this is a new claim, not the old one being doubted.

D.why: This is the explanation offered for the steady inflow, so it sits on the new-evidence side. It is also hedged with 'apparently', which makes it a poor candidate for the doubted view.

items.subtype_name: What does the new evidence cast doubt on?
items.stimulus: Because elite sprinters leave the blocks within about 0.15 seconds of the starting gun, coaches have often credited them with unusually fast nerve signaling in general. In a laboratory test, however, sprinters and nonathletes pressed a button in response to either a flash of light or a sharp click. The sprinters responded to the click markedly faster than the nonathletes did but responded to the light no faster. These results cast doubt on the idea that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: sprinters have trained themselves to react quickly to sharp sounds.
sprinters' fast starts come from quicker nerve signaling in general.
sprinters react to sharp sounds faster than nonathletes typically do.
sprinters' nerve signaling is slower overall than that of nonathletes.
items.explanation: A general speed advantage would show up for any stimulus. The sprinters were faster only for the sound and matched the nonathletes for the light. That attacks 'in general', so the coaches' broad claim is what's doubted.

A.why: The test shows a difference, not where it came from. Training is one explanation, and the passage never rules out others, such as sprinters being selected for this ability. That is an extra step.

C.why: The results support this. It is the finding on the new side of the 'however', not the old claim being questioned.

D.why: You saw the general advantage fail and swung to the opposite. Responding 'no faster' to light is not the same as being slower, and they were faster to sound, so 'slower overall' isn't supported.
